Sincere
sin-SEER
adjective
From the Latin sincerus, “clean, pure, unmixed, whole”; hence unadulterated, without any foreign or corrupting thing. The old fancy derived it from sine cera, “without wax,” of pure honey.

Biblical Definition

Sincere in the KJV keeps its oldest and purest force: unmixed, unadulterated, without any foreign thing folded in. It is not first a word about honest feeling but about unmingled substance — that is sincere which has nothing added to corrupt it. So Peter bids the newborn to “desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2) — pure milk, unwatered and undrugged, with no mingling of man’s doctrine to sicken the child. Paul prays that the Philippians “may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ” (Php 1:10), a heart of one metal and not an alloy. He appoints the same purity to the conscience: “in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world” (2Co 1:12) — a walk with nothing double in it, no craft folded under the profession. And he sets the feast of the church under the figure of unleavened bread: “let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1Co 5:8). Leaven is the foreign thing that spreads and sours; sincerity is the loaf with no leaven in it. Old writers loved the fancy that sincerus meant honey without wax; the sense is exact either way: the sincere heart is pure through and through, the same in the dark as in the light, one thing all the way down.

Webster 1828 Definition

Pure; unmixed; unadulterated; genuine through and through.

From Latin sincerus, “clean, whole, unmingled.”

An old fancy read it sine cera, “without wax,” of pure honey.

Key Scripture

1Pe 2:2 — "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:"

Php 1:10 — "That ye may approve things that are excellent; that ye may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ;"

2Co 1:12 — "For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward."

1Co 5:8 — "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."

Modern Corruption

An honest drift from “pure and unmixed” toward mere “honest feeling”; the word recovers purity of substance — the unleavened heart, the unwatered word.

expand to see more

The modern ear takes “sincere” to mean well-meant, heartfelt, honestly intended — a word about the warmth of a feeling. The AV means first a purity of substance: that is sincere which has nothing foreign mixed into it. A man may be sincere in the modern sense — earnest, heartfelt — and be sincerely wrong; but the biblical sincere milk of the word is milk with no poison stirred in, and the sincere heart is one metal and not an alloy. To reduce the word to good intentions is to lose the whole force of the unleavened loaf.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is purity through and through — the heart the same in the dark as in the light, with no leaven of malice folded under the profession. Paul prays the saints be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ, and bids them keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. The mark of a sincere man is not the strength of his feeling but the singleness of his substance: no craft hidden, no double aim, no foreign thing corrupting the whole. And such purity is not native to us; it is the sincere milk of the word that grows it, and the grace of God, not fleshly wisdom, by which alone a man walks sincere in the world.
